A poll is only as accurate as the poll taker makes it. A biased polling outlet will inherently bias the results of the poll by using tactics such as: limiting polling area, using a small sample size, asking loaded questions, and misrepresenting the data. This isn't even going into out and out lying. Consider how many graphs you've seen where the gap between two bars are enormous, but the scale shows that the difference of two or so percentage points.

Polling is a science if it is done accurately, namely, properly randomizing the sample, properly filtering the population to get your desired sample, getting a big enough sample, and finally asking unbiased questions. However, because there are so many variables when it comes to polling, it is very easy to manipulate and obfuscate the manipulation.

In short, no, ever trust any poll out of hand, even from a trustworthy source. Always verify before putting trust in it, but questioning its methods and outcome. Like all sciences, take every report as a single data point, and wait until the method is replicated and confirmed by another independent source.

Polling and surveys are poor tools. They are primarily used because we have little else to choose from.

Any poll or survey is going to have bias built-in - self-selection. People who can't be bothered to do anything with it, won't. And a lot of people can't be bothered. So right there you are, in many cases, biasing it by people who are particularly opinionated or have some kind of an axe to grind. If it's a poll that's large enough you probably also have people who like to screw with the numbers in there for whatever reason, as well, and this all assumes that people will answer accurately with their true thoughts, not with what comes off the top of their head in five seconds, and that they actually bother to read the questions in the first place.

I would use them as a vague indication as to what's going on, but I would always keep the caveat in mind that this is a very distorted picture of reality with many gotchas and caveats laced throughout, and cannot be interpreted as anywhere near 100% accurate. There are reasons there are so many polls by so many different organizations, and there is a reason why all of them give different numbers. Those reasons are not necessarily the dishonesty of the organization.

EDIT: One additional note - some things, such as how many people have landlines, might in fact be accurate. It depends on who is reporting it. If you have, say, phone company data, it might be mostly accurate, particularly if there is little incentive for the company to lie or distort the data in the first place. If you rely on a random poll, that's another story.

Be aware of the methodology. If the poll is anonymous, you'll be more truthful answers than if it's done on a street corner/on Facebook. Also, bear in mind the likelihood of groups of people to actually vote.

Polling is tangentially related to my job so I have both a personal and professional interest in polling failures.

If you want a US example, the presidential election of 1936 was a spectacular failure of election polling. The Literary Digest ran a poll that predicted Alf Landon would easily be Franklin Roosevelt. Two things went wrong: firstly, more Republicans subscribed than Democrats. Second, the responses had to be mailed back to the magazine, so only people interested in politics would bother to respond. Since then, pollsters have known that they need to survey a large and mixed sample of people.

It's all about the pollster. There are good ones (rare) and there are bad ones (the rest). Statistics is complex and in many ways half parts art and half parts science. One way you can determine a pollsters competence is looking at their predictions immediately predating a result. Here are Gallup's presidential prediction vs actual results over a period of decades. You can see following some years of growing pains they tended to start putting out some rather accurate polls, but even they have missed pretty hard at times. They had Romney winning by a point. Instead Obama won by 4 - that's a statistically significant error and consequently they completely reevaluated their methodology, but could not seem to find any flaws. As a result of this they've chosen to not cover the primaries with regular candidate polls, and may not even cover the 2016 election.

I think the general answer is that if Gallup has acknowledged they can't do it right, don't expect the other pollsters to be able to do better. Their answers are going to be in the general ballpark, but when it gets down to differences of a few percents it doesn't mean as much as it should.

libtcod is a free, fast, portable and uncomplicated API for roguelike developers providing an advanced true color console, input, and lots of other utilities frequently used in roguelikes.

Very impressive, this library. It looks great, it runs great. The only thing I don't like is the build system, which isn't the standard automake `./configure && make`. Not hard to figure out, but I'm just going to offer this set of instructions as a convenience. (Partly *my own* convenience, since I like my hoops pre-jumped-through.)

hg clone https://bitbucket.org/libtcod/libtcod cd libtcod make -f build/makefile-linux

There's no `install` target in the makefiles, so maybe make a note that you put these here manually, if you ever mean to uninstall this library:

sudo ln -s $(realpath libtcod.so) /usr/local/lib/libtcod.so.1 sudo ln -s $(realpath libtcodxx.so) /usr/local/lib/libtcodxx.so.1

There's also a sample project that you can build to make sure everything works. The samples makefile expects you to have UPX, which is a tool that compresses executables. If you don't have UPX, you can either put a dummy script in your PATH, or else delete each UPX line from `build/makefile-linux`. (There are only ~4.)

Having done that:

make -f build-makefile-samples-linux

Passing `-j4` *worked on my machine*
